      <title>California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state</link>
      <description><p>Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded</p><p>Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.</p><p>Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits</p><p>Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.</p><p>The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/19/baobab-five-trees-south-africa-dug-up-export-blocked-georgia-aoe">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds</p><p>One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.</p><p>In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/21/excitement-unease-haiti-el-salvador-troops-gangs-war-bukele</link>

But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.</p><p>In 2024, as the surrounding city was <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2024/nov/19/inside-port-au-prince-haiti-the-capital-where-gangs-have-taken-over-podcast">almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs</a>, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/21/louisiana-mississippi-hiking-trail-crossbow-murder-charges</link>
      <description><p>Jared Schurr arrested in Mississippi after Lizeht Rodriguez and Woodrow Scott died in otherwise unrelated killings</p><p>A man recently strangled a woman to death whom he did not know along a hiking trail north of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/new-orleans">New Orleans</a> – then killed his co-worker with a crossbow two days later before being arrested in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/mississippi">Mississippi</a> after a police chase, authorities allege.</p><p>Jared Schurr, 36, faces counts of second-degree murder in the killings of Lizeht Rodriguez, 24, and Woodrow Scott, 37, on 11 and 13 November, respectively, investigators <a href="https://www.facebook.com/stpso/posts/pfbid032S7CyaS1FkGyaLe4gJQjfADxy9W4o6EChy9tPZyNydPejgV4USdeFKcwYVBiWznel">said</a> on Saturday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/21/louisiana-mississippi-hiking-trail-crossbow-murder-charges">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/21/trump-contractors-congress-executive-order</link>
      <description><p>Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts</p><p>Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.</p><p>The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says.
